t: Mandaeans believe in one God, Hayyi Rabbi, the Great Life, whose symbol is living water, and for that reason they need to live near rivers; baptism in flowing water is performed every Sunday.
Mandaeans revere Adam, Seth, Noah, Shem and above all John the Baptist, whom they hold to be the greatest and final prophet, and they regard Jesus as a false prophet.
Mandaeism does not allow conversion, and the community has shrunk in Iraq: by 2007 about 5,000 Mandaeans remained there, as many fled the turmoil that followed the invasion of 2003.
dyk: Mandaeans call every river fit for baptism Yardena, after the River Jordan, and every mandi, their place of worship, must stand beside a river or, in modern buildings, hold a bath in its place.
ev: According to the Haran Gawaita, Nasoraean disciples of John the Baptist leave Jerusalem and migrate to Media, reportedly because of persecution
The oldest Mandaean texts, lead amulets, date from about this century, and the colophons of the Left Ginza attest Mandaeans in the late Parthian Empire
At the start of the Muslim conquest of Mesopotamia the Mandaean leader Anush bar Danqa is said to have shown the Ginza Rabba to the Muslim authorities, an account likely apocryphal
Al-Hasan ibn Bahlul, citing the vizier ibn Muqla, is the earliest source to apply the name Sabians to the Mandaeans
The Dominican friar Riccoldo da Monte di Croce meets the Mandaeans in Mesopotamia and is possibly the first European source on the religion
Cholera in Shushtar eliminates most Mandaean religious authorities there; two acolytes reestablish the priesthood at Suq al-Shuyukh
Many Mandaeans flee Iraq after the invasion and the rise in sectarian violence by extremists; by 2007 about 5,000 remain
Mandaeans begin settling in Worcester, Massachusetts, where a community of about 2,500 now lives

f.origin: According to the Haran Gawaita, Nasoraean disciples of John the Baptist left Jerusalem in the first century CE and settled in southern Mesopotamia; scholars dispute whether the origin lay in Israel or in Mesopotamia.
f.founder: none: Mandaeans hold Adam to be the founder of the religion and John the Baptist its greatest and final prophet, who renews and reforms an ancient faith; they do not regard John as its founder.
f.scriptures: The Ginza Rabba (Left and Right Ginza), the Qulasta prayerbook, the Draša d-Yahya or Book of John, the Haran Gawaita, the Diwan Abatur and the Book of the Zodiac, in Mandaic.
f.followers: Between 60,000 and 100,000 worldwide; 60,000 to 70,000 in 2007, when about 5,000 remained in Iraq; around 10,000 in Australia.
